paragraphs.heading: What a battery is
paragraphs.text: An electric battery is a supply of electric power. It is built from one or more electrochemical cells, with outside connections so it can run electrical devices. The word once meant a device with several cells, but today a single cell counts too. Batteries range from tiny cells in hearing aids and wristwatches to room-sized banks that give backup or emergency power to telephone exchanges and data centres.

paragraphs.heading: Chemical energy into electricity
paragraphs.text: A battery turns chemical energy straight into electrical energy. Inside it, reactants holding more energy change into products holding less, and the difference in free energy goes out to the circuit as electricity. In many cases that energy is the difference in bond energies between the metals, oxides or molecules taking part. The design matters: the reaction can only run when electrons travel through the outside part of the circuit.

paragraphs.heading: Two terminals
paragraphs.text: While a battery is delivering power, its negative terminal is called the anode and its positive terminal the cathode. Electrons come out of the negative terminal. When a load is connected, they flow around the circuit to the positive terminal, where they drive a redox reaction by attracting positively charged ions, called cations. At the anode, metal atoms have electrons taken away, which is oxidation. At the cathode, cations gain electrons, which is reduction.

paragraphs.heading: Inside a cell
paragraphs.text: A battery is made of some number of voltaic cells. Each cell has two half-cells joined in series by an electrolyte, a conducting substance that holds metal cations. One half-cell contains the negative electrode, which negatively charged ions, called anions, move towards. The other contains the positive electrode, which the cations move towards.

paragraphs.heading: Single-use and rechargeable
paragraphs.text: Primary batteries are used once and then thrown away, because discharging changes their electrode materials for good. The alkaline battery in a flashlight is a common example. Secondary batteries can be drained and charged again many times: running current through them in reverse brings the electrodes back to their original makeup. The lead–acid battery in cars with internal combustion engines and the lithium-ion batteries in portable electronics and electric cars are both of this kind.

paragraphs.heading: From jars to the voltaic pile
paragraphs.text: Benjamin Franklin first used the word in 1749 for a set of linked Leyden jars, borrowing the military term for weapons working together. In 1800 the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta built the first electrochemical battery, the voltaic pile. It was a stack of copper and zinc plates with brine-soaked paper disks between them, and it gave a steady current for a long time. Volta did not grasp that chemical reactions made his voltage, and he saw the corrosion at the electrodes as a nuisance. Michael Faraday showed in 1834 that this corrosion was an unavoidable part of how the cells work.

paragraphs.heading: Wet cells to dry cells
paragraphs.text: In 1836 the British chemist John Frederic Daniell invented the Daniell cell. It became the first practical source of electricity and was widely used to power telegraph networks. Cells like it held a liquid electrolyte that could leak or spill, often in fragile glass jars, so they were no good for portable devices. Near the end of the 1800s the dry cell replaced the liquid with a paste, and portable electrical devices became practical.

paragraphs.heading: A weakness and a boom
paragraphs.text: Batteries store much less energy for their mass than common fuels such as gasoline. In cars this is partly balanced out, because electric motors turn electrical energy into mechanical work more efficiently than combustion engines do. Battery demand rose by 30% a year between 2010 and 2018, reaching 180 GWh. Major reasons for this growth include electric transport and large-scale use in electricity grids.
